analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's exemption from federal antitrust price-fixing laws.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, insurance companies have been exempt from most federal antitrust laws under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, meaning they could agree on prices among themselves with far less risk of prosecution. This bill would have made federal antitrust enforcement apply to insurance companies — letting regulators challenge price-fixing and market allocation — unless a state actively supervised the conduct, and would have kept the exemption only for routine activities like sharing historical loss data and standardized policy forms.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses that buy insurance — health, auto, home, and liability coverage — who would benefit if insurers competing on price were less able to coordinate their rates. Small insurers without market power could also gain from fairer competition.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so federal antitrust law, including the Federal Trade Commission Act, applies to the insurance industry's methods of competition unless a state actively supervises the conduct in question [S2] [S3].
It would let enforcers challenge agreements among insurers that allocate markets or set or restrain prices, which the bill's carve-out language specifically excludes from any protection [S3].

The exemption would be preserved only for ordinary informational and standardization activities, such as compiling aggregated historical loss data and shared policy forms, so routine industry cooperation would not be threatened [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose their long-standing protection from federal antitrust prosecution for anti-competitive conduct, and could face lawsuits or enforcement actions over coordinated pricing.

drawbacks.text: Critics of McCarran-Ferguson repeal arguments point to the bill's own carve-outs: sharing aggregated historical loss data and standardized policy forms remains protected [S3], and defenders of the exemption argue those practices lower premiums, especially in medical malpractice and auto insurance markets.

The bill still preserves the exemption where a state actively supervises the conduct [S3], so the practical effect on pricing could be smaller than full repeal, and overlapping federal and state enforcement could raise compliance costs that insurers pass through to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing a blanket exemption that lets insurers coordinate pricing without federal antitrust risk — outweighs the compliance costs, particularly because the bill carefully protects legitimate data-sharing and standardization. The main uncertainty is that the state-supervision carve-out limits how much would actually change in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2006, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Senator Arlen Specter introduced the bill on September 29, 2006, joined by three cosponsors, one Republican and two Democrats [S1] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies are better off: the antitrust exemption this bill would have lifted remains on the books, and the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-PA), bill sponsor and then-chairman of the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which he chaired, but never advanced it to a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the Congress expired with it still pending.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Insurers benefiting from the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal antitrust repeal proposals of this kind, which threatened their exemption from price-fixing liability.

sides.party_line_note: The four original sponsors split two Republicans and two Democrats, so the bill had support from both parties from day one, but opposition likely ran through inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped insurers' federal antitrust immunity for anti-competitive conduct such as coordinated pricing and market allocation. Losing the exemption exposes them to enforcement and lawsuits, and their interest in keeping the status quo runs against consumers who pay the coordinated prices.
